summary:
We are a team from Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia. In our country many herder families live hours away from the nearest hospital, so they have to judge for themselves when a health problem is serious. Astronauts on the way to Mars will be in the same situation, only much further away: a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to 20 minutes one way.

The Ether is a web app that helps astronauts check their own health every day. It learns what is normal for each crew member during the first two weeks, then watches for slow changes in sleep, reaction time, mood, teamwork, heart rate, blood pressure, exercise and radiation dose. When something keeps drifting, it explains what changed, why it matters, what to do right now, and whether the astronaut, the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon on Earth should act.

The daily check takes about three minutes. The pulse and reaction checks need only the device's camera and screen; blood pressure, glucose and temperature come from the standard medical kit and are typed in.
details:
THE PROBLEM WE FOCUSED ON

While reading NASA's Human Research Program pages, we noticed that the dangerous health problems on a long mission are usually not sudden. Sleep gets a little shorter every night, blood pressure creeps up, bones weaken when exercise is skipped. These changes are easy to miss, and astronauts may not want to report that they feel tired. NASA also points out that the five hazards of spaceflight make each other worse, so looking at one number at a time is not enough. On a Mars mission, the crew has to notice these things themselves.

WHAT THE ETHER DOES

1. Learns your normal. For every person and every indicator, the app builds a personal normal range from the first 14 days instead of using a population average.

2. Catches slow drift. An alert only appears when a change lasts (3 of the last 5 days) or a safety limit is crossed. We added a "hidden fatigue" check: if sleep and reaction time get worse while the person keeps reporting a good mood, the app flags it gently to the crew medical officer.

3. Explains and tells you who should act. Every alert shows the readings behind it, the NASA risk it is linked to, a short checklist, and one of three levels: handle it yourself, involve the crew medical officer, or contact the flight surgeon on Earth. For Earth-level alerts the app drafts a message and shows how long the signal will take to arrive.

4. Daily 3-minute check. A camera pulse reading (all processing stays on the device), a reaction-time test similar to the PVT used in sleep research, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, oxygen, sleep, mood and a "crew pulse" question about teamwork. Each step has a short "Why this test?" note with sources.

5. Body map. A clickable figure where each body system turns green, amber or red. Tapping it shows what that system does, how spaceflight affects it, recent values compared with your normal, and what to do.

6. Mission clock. A slider across a simulated 180-day trip to Mars. You can drag it to see a solar storm on day 40, hidden fatigue around day 70, a heart and blood pressure change around day 95, and missed exercise later in the mission.

7. Crew quests. Small daily goals (exercise, sleep, check-in, time with the crew) that the whole crew completes together, without ranking people against each other.

WHY IT MATTERS

NASA already collects many of these measures in studies like Spaceflight Standard Measures and ARCHeR, which look at sleep, cognition, well-being and crew interaction. Those studies are built to help researchers improve future protocols. We wanted to give the crew something they can use themselves during the mission, every day, without needing a doctor or a connection to Earth. The same idea also fits remote places on Earth, so we added a Mongolian mode for herder families as a second use case.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Framer Motion and IndexedDB, deployed on Vercel. There is no login and no database: health data stays on the device. Three small server routes fetch NASA open data: JPL Horizons (Earth–Mars distance for the signal-delay estimate), DONKI (real 2024 solar particle events replayed on the mission timeline) and NASA POWER (real 2024 winter weather for the Mongolian herder scenario). The health logic is covered by 100 unit tests and the app by 41 end-to-end tests.

LIMITS WE ARE HONEST ABOUT

The crew data is simulated (four fictional crew members). Thresholds come from the sources listed below, and anything we could not source is labelled "demo parameter" in the app. This is a prototype, not a medical device.
